overview: This exercise connected Windows Remote Access configuration with interface roles, policy and accounting. I also worked through a client destination-name mistake before checking the server’s active connection view.
environment: Windows Server DC01 and Windows 10 client
Two virtual adapters: Private and Public
Remote Access, RRAS and Network Policy Server
VMware virtual NAT and internal segments

steps.title: Add the second network adapter
steps.description: I added a second adapter to the server VM and attached it to the VMware NAT network. Public is the lab’s interface label; it is not evidence of an Internet-facing public address.

steps.title: Install the access and policy roles
steps.description: I installed Remote Access with VPN (RAS) and Routing, together with Network Policy and Access Services.

steps.title: Select the VPN-only deployment path
steps.description: I used the Remote Access setup path for VPN deployment and opened the Routing and Remote Access console.

steps.title: Enable VPN access and NAT in RRAS
steps.description: I selected Custom configuration, enabled VPN access and NAT, and started the RRAS service.

steps.title: Name the interfaces clearly
steps.description: I renamed the adapters Private and Public before binding NAT so their intended roles were easier to distinguish.

steps.title: Configure the external NAT interface
steps.description: I selected Public as the external interface and enabled NAT on it.

steps.title: Configure the private NAT interface
steps.description: I identified Private as connected to the internal network and reviewed the NAT list with both interfaces present.

steps.title: Set the NPS connection policy
steps.description: I updated the matching RRAS network policy to grant access under the lab’s VPN dial-up connection conditions.

steps.title: Enable connection accounting
steps.description: I configured local Inbox Accounting in Remote Access reporting so the service could retain connection information.

steps.title: Create and correct the client profile
steps.description: I created the Windows VPN connection profile. When its destination name failed, I compared the entered hostname with the intended server name and corrected the typo.

steps.title: Check client connection status
steps.description: After correcting the destination, I recorded the profile’s Connected state on the client.

steps.title: Inspect the server session
steps.description: I reviewed the active connection in Remote Client Status. The capture identifies PPTP and includes session statistics; the user identity field is removed from the display copy.

checks.title: RRAS interfaces and policy
checks.description: The captures show both NAT interfaces, the selected NPS access policy and the accounting configuration.

checks.title: Client and server connection state
checks.description: The client shows Connected and the server lists an active PPTP session.

checks.title: Hostname correction
checks.description: The report records the initially mistyped destination and its correction before connection succeeded.

lessons: Interface labels and NAT bindings should make the packet path understandable.
A destination-name error can look like a service failure; name resolution is an early troubleshooting check.
A connected tunnel does not by itself establish strong security or a restrictive access policy.
PPTP is obsolete. A current remote-access design should use suitable modern protocols and separate the gateway role from a domain controller.
scope: PPTP, broad lab policy settings and combined server roles are recorded as training choices. I do not present this as a secure Internet deployment, and no account password or VPN key is included.

troubleshooting.title: The VPN destination did not resolve
troubleshooting.symptom: The initial client profile used the wrong server name and domain suffix.
troubleshooting.action: I compared the profile with the intended server identity, corrected the destination and retried the connection.
troubleshooting.result: The client displayed Connected and the server recorded the session.
